name: Bunbury Airwave
year: Installation attempted December 2019 (failed during install) [R1][R5]; concept development began ~2008-2009 [R2]
type: Inflatable dome-shaped rubber (Hypalon) 'air bladder' artificial surf reef, anchored with sand ballast and filled with air/sand, glued (not welded) seams [R3][R9][R8] | Per the founder (interview 2026-10-10), the FINAL design is filled with sand instead of air, because the engineers found air did not respond well with the waves [R25]; this differs from the air/sand fill described above (see sources_disagree).
purpose: Create a reliable, rideable wave at a beach with swell but poor bathymetry ('closeouts'); position Bunbury as a surfing destination alternative to nearby Margaret River, attract competitions/tourism, give local surfers a place to progress [R1][R2][R6]
size: Base diameter 12 m (≈40 ft) [R1][R2][R3][R6]; height above seabed given as 2 m in most sources but 1.6 m at its highest point in one dedicated preview article [R1][R2][R3][R6][R9]; sited ~30–45 m offshore in ~1 m of water at low tide [R2][R3][R9]; filled with washed coarse beach sand (140 tonnes) plus air [R9][R8]
cost: City of Bunbury committed A$75,000 as a council sponsorship (approved June 2019) [R1][R2]; total project cost reported as ~US$400,000 including installation by one source and ~US$350,000 by another — sources disagree on the total figure [R3][R10]
cost_usd_approx: ~350,000–400,000 (total project, disputed between sources); A$75,000 (~US$50,000) of that was the confirmed City of Bunbury contribution [R1][R2][R3][R10] ASSUMPTION: the A$75,000 = ~US$50,000 conversion uses an unsourced rate (~0.67); not confirmed against a rate table.
financed_by: City of Bunbury council sponsorship (A$75,000, approved June 2019) [R1][R2]; an August 2018 Kickstarter crowdfunding campaign by Waveco failed to raise enough [R3]; remainder via Waveco/Bottegal investors [R5]
motivation: Bunbury sits near Margaret River, a premier surf destination, but Back Beach had swell without the bathymetry to shape it into rideable waves [R1][R2][R6]. Waveco founder Troy Bottegal had spent roughly a decade developing the inflatable-bladder concept and wanted a real-world test site [R2][R10]; the City of Bunbury under Mayor Gary Brennan saw it as a low-cost way to brand the town as a surfing destination and draw competitions and tourism [R2].
designer: Troy Bottegal, inventor and sole patent holder, director of Waveco Pty Ltd (Dunsborough, WA); conceived the idea after watching a dome-shaped ('oyster') light fitting create ripples in a bathtub [R6][R10]
contractor: Waveco Pty Ltd; installation used three divers and a boat [R9]; fabrication was originally overseas, later moved to a Western Australian manufacturer after the 2019 failure [R5][R8]
status_now: Torn along a glued seam during installation, ~90% complete, mid-December 2019; the partially-inflated bladder was removed from the water within about three days per most sources, though one source (Bottegal, 2020-07-09) separately says it was removed in half a day — the two figures conflict [R1][R5][R8][R18]. A second Airwave prototype install, needing a further ~A$300,000, was being planned for December 2020 [R18]; no source confirms whether it happened or succeeded. A 2022-03-22 article quotes Bottegal saying the Airwave would be 'back in the water in time for Summer, 2024' after relocating fabrication to a WA manufacturer [R8]. A Waveco Instagram post from June 2024 shows an active Bunbury Back Beach surf-cam [R11]. By September 2025, Waveco's own site/Instagram show its active Bunbury proposal has shifted to a 'granite artificial reef' (rock) design at a dedicated project site (bunburyartificialreef.info), framed around coastal-erosion protection rather than surf amenity [R20] — no source confirms the original inflatable Airwave was ever successfully reinstalled; status as of research date is unconfirmed for the inflatable Airwave specifically, and Waveco's current Bunbury-facing project appears to be a different (granite) technology [R8][R11][R18][R20] Addition 2026-10-10: per the founder (interview 8 Oct 2026), they are now going for concrete [R25]. Not independently confirmed; consistent in direction with the rock/granite proposal in [R20] but not the same material.
hover_text: A 12 m inflatable rubber 'air bladder' surf reef (A$75,000 council funding; total project ~US$350–400,000, disputed) that tore along a glued seam during its December 2019 installation off Bunbury Back Beach, WA, and was pulled from the water within days: it failed, because it was never completed and no independent source documents rideable waves on it [R1][R3][R8][R18]. The developer calls it 'not a failure' and says it 'successfully created peeling waves', but its own page misdates the install to 2018 and no independent report supports the wave claim [R21]; by 2025 its Bunbury proposal is a different (granite/rock) design [R20].
design_as_planned: A 12 m-diameter, dome-shaped inflatable rubber bladder anchored to the seabed with sand ballast, filled with air/sand/water, sited ~30–45 m offshore in ~1 m of water at low tide [R2][R3][R9]. It was meant to 'lift, peak, and hold the swell to create a concave, tapered wall of water that retains its shape as it peels toward the beach' [R19], producing an A-frame peak with left and right breaks where there had previously only been closeouts [R3]. Bottegal modelled the intended wave on Thunderbomb, a wave in Nicaragua [R4]. It was designed to work across roughly 2–8 ft swell, with expected ride length ~40 m / 26 seconds, over an estimated 150 rideable-swell days per year [R2][R3][R9]. A hard-wired webcam and a planned 12-month University of Western Australia scientific study were part of the design [R9]. The reversibility/removability of the inflatable design (not ecological habitat creation) was the explicit environmental/cost pitch — 'if they don't do what you want them to do... they take half a day to move' [R10].
as_built_vs_design: Construction was reported 'halfway complete' in October 2019 against a November 2019 install target [R4]; installation slipped to December 2019, and divers/boat crew got the bladder to ~90% complete (deployed but not fully anchored) when an unexpectedly large, deep offshore swell drove strong undertow through the line-up during the final fill/anchoring phase, tearing a glued seam [R1][R5][R6]. The tear was along the seam, not the rubber itself [R1]; the underlying cause was the choice of Hypalon rubber, which could not be welded and so had to be glued — a joint that could not withstand pump pressure during the final fill [R8]. The bladder was removed within about three days (one conflicting account says half a day) [R1][R5][R8][R18]. The reef therefore was never completed to its designed, fully-anchored, surfable state (card author's inference from the ~90 % complete, not fully anchored state in [R1][R5]). Addition 2026-10-10: the founder says the final design used SAND instead of AIR as the fill, because the engineers found air did not respond well with the waves; the failure was a seam that opened up a couple of days after installation (not a tear during the fill phase), and until then it worked "amazingly" [R25, notes as reported by Lior]. Both accounts kept; see sources_disagree. [R25]
outcome: Installation was not completed: the bladder tore and was pulled from the water, unsurfable in its intended form [R1][R5][R8]. During the brief period it was partially in the water, Bottegal later reported that 'a wave did break on it... peeled nearly all the way to the beach... created a 0.75 metre wave' — the only quantified wave-performance data found, describing a small, uncontrolled result rather than a validated trial [R8]. No formal UWA study results were found; the planned 12-month study appears never to have started [R9]. A second prototype installation was being planned for December 2020 with a further A$300,000 [R18], but no source confirms it happened or succeeded. A 2022 article promised a Summer 2024 relaunch after moving fabrication to WA [R8]; a June 2024 Instagram post shows an active surf-cam [R11]; but by September 2025 Waveco's active Bunbury-facing project had shifted to a different, granite (rock) reef design aimed at coastal-erosion protection [R20]. No source listed in References confirms (negative finding of this card) the inflatable Airwave was ever successfully completed and operating as a surf reef at Bunbury. Addition 2026-10-10: founder says the structure worked perfectly until a seam opened a couple of days after installation [R25]; the card keeps the independent record (tear during installation, removal within about three days) and records the disagreement.
why_worked_or_failed: Failure mechanism (installation, Dec 2019): an unexpectedly deep offshore swell during the final anchoring/fill phase generated strong undertow that flexed the bladder, concentrating stress on a glued seam [R1][R5][R6]. The underlying materials cause was the use of Hypalon rubber, which cannot be welded; the glued seams used instead could not withstand pressure reached during the final pump/fill stage [R8]. This was a materials/fabrication-method failure compounded by an installation-timing/weather-window problem, rather than a wave-performance or siting failure — the reef never reached a state where its surf-shaping performance could be properly judged (the card author's synthesis of [R1][R5][R6][R8]; the classification is an inference, not a source statement). Addition 2026-10-10: founder account (personal communication): the seam opened a couple of days after installation, and the fill choice for the final design moved from air to sand because air did not respond well with the waves [R25]. This agrees that a seam was the failure point, but differs on timing and on whether the structure was complete (card author's comparison of [R25] with [R1][R5][R8]).
unexpected_results: The one recorded moment of the Airwave functioning — before the tear forced its removal — reportedly produced a wave that 'peeled nearly all the way to the beach' and reached about 0.75 m, an unplanned, brief glimpse of the concept working, per Bottegal's later account [R8]. No sources document fishing-pressure effects, ecological colonization, rip-current changes, safety incidents, or litigation connected to this installation in the sources listed in References (negative finding of this card) — plausible given the structure was never operational for an extended period (card author's inference). Local news noted reputational 'deflation' for Bunbury when the trial failed on a high-profile install day [R1]. Addition 2026-10-10: the founder told Lior that until the seam opened it "worked amazingly, perfect waves" [R25, personal communication, notes as reported by Lior]. This is a self-interested, unrecorded, second-hand account; no independent report, photo or video confirms it, and it is larger than the single 0.75 m wave in [R8].
could_be_better: From Waveco/the designer's own account: the identified fix was materials and fabrication method — move away from glued Hypalon seams (relocating manufacture to a WA-based manufacturer) and secure fresh investment before re-attempting installation [R8]. Bottegal framed the setback as a timing/weather issue (an unplanned deep swell during the vulnerable, partially-anchored install phase) rather than a fundamental design flaw, maintaining '100 percent' confidence the concept would work [R6]. Detailed surfer/commentator critique was not found in the sources successfully retrieved for this research (negative finding of this card) [see dossier for blocked forum sources]. Addition 2026-10-10: the founder says the next version goes to CONCRETE (no detail on design, date or site) [R25]; the final design as described fills with sand, not air [R25].
relevance_to_israel: Bunbury sits on a microtidal WA coast (tidal range roughly ~1 m or less) [R13], broadly comparable in scale to the Mediterranean's small tidal range at Haifa — not itself a factor implicated in the Bunbury failure, but relevant to sizing an Israeli pilot in a similarly low-tide setting. Wave climate differs in kind: Bunbury/SW WA faces Southern Ocean groundswell (~150 rideable-swell days/year) [R9], far more energetic than the Eastern Mediterranean's short-period, wind-driven seas off Haifa. What transfers: (1) the low-cost [R10], rapidly-removable [R18] inflatable concept is attractive for a wave-poor, low-tidal-range coast like Israel's, avoiding large capital commitment before wave performance is proven; (2) the documented failure mode — glued (not welded) seam material failing under dynamic swell/undertow loading during the vulnerable partially-anchored installation phase — is a fabrication/installation-window risk any Israeli inflatable-reef pilot would need to solve first, independent of local wave/tide conditions (failure mode: [R1][R8]; the transfer is the card author's inference); (3) because Israel's swell energy is much lower than SW Australia's (card author's general statement, (unsourced) here), a device sized for Bunbury's 2–8 ft face range (UNSOURCED figure: no reference in this card gives it; treat as unverified) may be oversized for Haifa's smaller everyday waves and would need dedicated re-sizing/modelling, not found in any source reviewed here. Tide range check: GHD (2021) Table 1 gives Port of Bunbury HAT 0.6 and LAT -0.6 m AHD, a range of 1.2 m, MSL +0.1 m AHD [R26], consistent with the sample-day heights of [R13] (which are one day only).

developer_account.quote: In 2018, we deployed a 150-tonne sand-slurry bladder at Bunbury’s Back Beach. While it successfully created peeling waves, a final-day overpressure event led to a seam split. It wasn't a failure—it was the catalyst for our next breakthrough.
developer_account.quote_check: verified verbatim in the raw page HTML on 2026-10-05 (the page uses a curly apostrophe in Bunbury’s and an em dash)
developer_account.independence: self-published by the developer; promotional; not independent
developer_account.adjacent_text: 'Post-2018, we pivoted. We designed and patented a modular concrete version of the Airwave... Simultaneously, we developed a conventional Granite ASR design.' (same page) [R21]

checks.independent_record: Installation was attempted in December 2019: it began the week of 9 Dec, a diver spotted the seam tear on the afternoon of Fri 13 Dec, and it was reported on Mon 16 Dec [R1][R5][R6][R7][R15]. Before that it had not been deployed: ABC (2019-06-13) said it was set to be installed in November [R2]; Tracks (2019-08-12) described a trial planned for mid-November and a crowd-funding campaign 'last year' [R23]; Raised Water Research (2019-10-14) said construction was half-way [R4]; Tracks (2019-11-15) said the live trial was 'some time in the next couple of months' [R9]; RWR's spot page says it was installed in December 2019 [R3]; ABC listen (2022-10-07) says 'In 2019 ... attempted to install' [R24]. The only 2018 events found are Waveco's failed Aug 2018 Kickstarter [R3] and a 'may be installed' preview [R19]. One outlier: the 2022 Bunbury Mail intro says 'four years since' and captions a supplied photo 'The original Bunbury Airwave in 2018' [R8]; that conflicts with every dated 2019 report above.

Sand-slurry fill is corroborated: Tracks 2019 ('washed, coarse beach sand... for that slurry') [R9]; Bottegal in the Bunbury Mail ('irrigate the sandslurry') [R8]; RWR ('partially filling it with sand', the rest water and air) [R3]; a local observer on Swellnet saw a slurry pump and hoses on the beach on 7 Dec 2019 [R15]. ABC and SurferToday call it 'filled with air' [R1][R7]; Tracks 2019 says 'a mixture of sand and air' [R9]; the card's 'air bladder anchored with sand ballast' fits all of these. The mass has no independent source: 140 tonnes in Tracks 2021 and the Bunbury Mail 2022, both reporting Bottegal [R22][R8]; '150T' in a forum summary of his Feb 2020 conference talk [R15]. So 140-150 t, developer-sourced only; the 7% gap is inside the developer's own statements.
checks.assessment: material and bladder type consistent; mass is developer-only, 140-150 t (card keeps 140 t)

checks.claim: 'While it successfully created peeling waves' (wave performance)
checks.independent_record: No independent report, photograph or video of surfable waves on the reef was found. ABC (2019-12-16) reports only the tear; it paraphrases a tourist as 'looking forward to riding whatever wave the Airwave produced' and beach-goers were told to keep away [R1]. RWR, SurferToday and The Inertia report no wave [R5][R6][R7]. The ABC video 11804314 shows the bladder on the seabed with a diver and no wave (card video notes). Tracks 2021 says the plan to webcast 'perfectly peeling waves' 'didn't quite play that way' [R22]; the webcam was not live for the install [R15]. The wave claim comes from the developer alone: Bottegal told the Bunbury Mail in 2022 that 'a wave did break' just before the tear, a 'lone wave' that 'peeled for about thirty metres' and 'created a 0.75 metre wave' seen by onlookers [R8] (his recollection 27 months later; no footage or named witness cited). Second-hand only: a Swellnet user quoting Waveco's Dec 2019 Instagram says the redesign reflects 'small wave action' observed during install, and a forum summary of his Feb 2020 talk lists 'Small Wave Peak' among positives [R15].
checks.assessment: not independently supported: at most ONE small wave (about 0.75 m, about 30 m long) reported by the developer himself, while the bladder was about 90% installed and not anchored; no ride by anyone, no footage found

checks.claim: 'a final-day overpressure event led to a seam split' (failure mechanism)
checks.independent_record: Seam split: confirmed; the tear was along a glued seam, not through the rubber [R1][R5][R8]. 'Final-day': the tear was spotted on about the fifth day of the install week (Fri 13 Dec) when, per ABC reporting Bottegal, it was '90 per cent complete' but 'not completely anchored' [R1][R7]; a local observer saw it 'partially filled' that afternoon [R15]. It never operated as a finished reef. 'Overpressure': this is the developer's own later explanation, and it changes. Dec 2019: an unexpected deep swell and undertow flexed the airbag against the seam [R1][R5][R7]. Oct 2021 (Tracks): sand pumped too heavily into one quadrant put too much pressure on one section of the skin, and the new valves avoid 'the same over pressurization problem' [R22]. Mar 2022 (Bunbury Mail): glued overlapped Hypalon seams plus 'full pump pressure applied to a confined space in the final fill phase' caused a tear in the back quadrant [R8]. No independent engineering report exists.
checks.assessment: partly supported: seam split true; 'overpressure' matches his 2021-22 accounts but not his 2019 one; 'final-day' makes an unfinished install sound like a completed deployment

checks.independent_record: Bottegal told the Bunbury Mail in Mar 2022 the prototype installation 'certainly was not a failure' [R8]. But Tracks (2021-10-08) writes that he 'readily admits that the first trial of his Airwave was a failure' (Tracks' paraphrase, not a direct quote) [R22]. Facts on record: the bladder tore during installation and was removed within days (reports range from about 5 hours to 3 days) [R8][R18][R15]; no completed trial and the planned 12-month UWA study never started [R9]; a second prototype (planned Dec 2020, about A$300,000 more needed) is not confirmed built [R18][R8]; the redesign has only been tank-tested [R22]; by 2025 Waveco's Bunbury proposal is a granite reef [R20]; and its own page says it 'pivoted' away from the rubber Airwave after 2018 [R21].
checks.assessment: a judgement, not a checkable fact; the record supports 'learning prototype' as the developer's framing but not 'success'

developer_account.overall: Of the four factual claims, one is contradicted (2018), one is consistent but developer-only on mass (150 t vs 140 t elsewhere), one is partly supported (seam split yes; 'final-day overpressure' reframes an unfinished install), and one has no independent support (successfully created peeling waves). The card verdict stays 'failed'.

verdict_reason: The structure tore along a glued seam during installation (spotted Fri 13 Dec 2019, about 90% installed and not fully anchored), was removed within days, and never operated as a completed reef [R1][R5][R8][R18]. No independent report, photo or video documents rideable waves on it; the only wave claim is the developer's own later account of one lone 0.75 m wave seen during installation [R8][R21]. The developer's page says the trial 'wasn't a failure' [R21], but it misdates the deployment to 2018 (it was December 2019), Tracks reported in 2021 that Bottegal 'readily admits' the first trial was a failure [R22], no second install is confirmed [R18][R8], and by 2025 Waveco's Bunbury proposal is a different (granite) design [R20]. Verdict kept as 'failed' after checking the developer's account (2026-10-05). Update 2026-10-10: the verdict stays failed, because the structure failed within days (a seam opened) and was never a durable reef [R1][R5][R25]. In fairness, the founder (Troy) told Lior the reef worked amazingly, with perfect waves, until the seam opened, and that the final design uses sand instead of air and the next step is concrete [R25, personal communication, notes as reported by Lior]. That is a developer statement and independent confirmation of surfable waves is still lacking. WHO DECIDED: the research agent that wrote this card (2026-09-24, re-checked 2026-10-05 against the developer's page, again 2026-10-10 after the interview); the orchestrator brief records the verdict as FAILED 'despite the developer's claim'. Lior has not overruled it.
